newsitem.title: USA: IRA responded to British peace offer with murders.
newsitem.headline: IRA responded to British peace offer with murders.

text.p: The IRA's murder of two policemen in Northern Ireland came days after Britain dramatically offered its political wing, Sinn Fein, a seat at peace talks if the guerrilla group observed a six-week written ceasefire, British officials said on Saturday.

Disclosure of the IRA's brusque rejection of the peace feelers helped to explain why Prime Minister Tony Blair reacted so furiously to the killings in the town of Lurgan on Monday, calling them callous and repugnant.

Blair enlisted the support of U.S. President Bill Clinton on Saturday to intensify pressure on the outlawed IRA to lay down its guns, warning that peace talks would continue with or without Sinn Fein.
Speaking after talks with Blair on the fringes of the annual summit of the Group of Seven industrialized nations, Clinton said he was appalled by the Lurgan murders.

"I frankly think now the ball is in Sinn Fein's court. We all have to decide. Everybody has decisions to make in life -- their decision is: are they going to be part of this peace process or not?" Clinton said.

He and Blair met shortly after a car bomb in Belfast slightly injured three people. Details of the explosion were sketchy, but British officials said they had evidence that a hardline pro-British Protestant group might have been involved.
Blair condemned what he called "another appalling terrorist act" and said it underlined the need to advance the tortuous process of bringing peace to the British-ruled province.
"What is essential is for Sinn Fein and everyone else to realise that if they want to be part of that process, they have got to engage in purely democratic means...
"It is now for those people who have been holding up this process to come in and make sure that we get that lasting settlement that people want," Blair said.

Officials called Clinton's support very welcome and said Britain spelled out its position on Sinn Fein's participation in peace talks in a note it gave the party after two rounds of exploratory talks last month.
"We were pretty clear," one official said, although he declined to comment publicly on the private disclosure by others of a six-week qualifying period.
The initiative showed that Blair was determined to try as hard as his Conservative predecessor John Major to make a breakthrough in Northern Ireland.
Officials acknowledged that the Lurgan killings had dealt a serious blow to the peace process but said Blair was determined to try to mobilize U.S. outrage to best advantage.
Aides sidestepped questions on whether the government would be prepared to put the six-week ceasefire formula back on the table.
"A ceasefire would have to be unequivocal, clear in word and deed, and with a clear commitment to the six Mitchell principles," a British official said.

Former Senator George Mitchell, who is chairing the multi-party peace talks in Belfast, drew up six democratic principles that the province's political parties must adhere to before gaining a seat at the negotiating table.

The IRA, which wants to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite the province with the Irish Republic to the south, ended a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996 with a series of attacks on the British mainland.
